headline: Nvidia's board probe into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative hit a tech sector already bruised by last week's AI rout, though broader markets looked steadier this morning. In healthcare, argenx's $1.15 billion buy of Unnatural Products and a pair of heart-drug failures lead the news.
watch: Nvidia's share price and any board or company update on the Huang investigation, plus further Wall Street talk about succession
US inflation data this week, with oil, gold and Treasury yields reacting
Iran and the Strait of Hormuz: whether the unconfirmed report of eased demands is confirmed or denied
Australian regulator action on private credit funds, and whether other managers face scrutiny
Italian and German bank deals: UniCredit-Commerzbank this month, the Intesa-Monte dei Paschi offer launch, and the Crédit Agricole proposal to Banco BPM

paragraphs.text: The main deal in biotech this morning is argenx buying Unnatural Products, a macrocycle company that began in a garage. Endpoints and Fierce Biotech put the value at up to about $1.15 billion, with $550 million paid upfront in cash and the rest contingent. Fierce says the target is partnered with Merck & Co. and Novartis, and that argenx is buying it for oral peptide capabilities. Argenx is best known for antibody-based immunology drugs, so the deal reads as a push into a different modality. The headlines don't give milestone terms or the target's pipeline stage, so judge the price carefully until the details emerge.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere in deals, ANI Pharmaceuticals is offering $560 million for Swedish drugmaker Egetis Therapeutics, whose Emcitate is the first and only approved treatment for MCT8 deficiency. Fierce Pharma Asia flags a potential $7.4 billion oncology deal between Boehringer Ingelheim and China's SBP Group, a 37-asset biosimilar collaboration between Fresenius and WuXi Biologics, and a roughly $1 billion molecular glue license from Hinova. Western buyers are clearly still sourcing from China. Siemens Healthineers is carving out its in vitro diagnostics business as a standalone company called Olyrian Diagnostics. Fierce Healthcare's October roundup mentions an $11 billion Chicago hospital merger and more health system and ambulatory surgery center deals. AbbVie is also putting £120 million into expanding its Oxford R&D site.

paragraphs.text: Cardiovascular news was bleak over the weekend. The NYT says two high-profile heart drugs were no better than placebo once full data came out Saturday, and doctors are debating whether the trial designs or the underlying hypotheses were at fault. Fierce Biotech reports Novartis's Lp(a) outcomes trial showed no efficacy at all, which raises doubts about upcoming readouts from Amgen and Eli Lilly in the same class. The headlines don't say whether the NYT piece covers the same drugs. STAT's opinion piece uses the failures to argue for skepticism about AI hype in drug discovery. For investors, the Lp(a) class now carries real read-across risk.

paragraphs.text: Some pipeline readouts were more positive. Vir says its hepatitis D combination worked in the first of three pivotal studies, with 44% of patients responding. Fierce says it hit the primary endpoint and gives Vir the first piece of an FDA filing planned for next year, in competition with Gilead and Mirum. Valneva's Shigella vaccine, from LimmaTech, cut infections in a phase 2 trial. Moderna had a mixed day. Fierce Pharma says third-quarter revenue of $1.3 billion far beat estimates and avoided a predicted loss, but its norovirus vaccine plans are in limbo after a phase 3 miss. Merck dropped a Sutro-partnered IL-2 drug as routine prioritization, and Novartis has confirmed more reported tumor cases in Zolgensma patients as advocacy groups ask for details.

paragraphs.text: On policy and commercial news, CMS has codified the Medicare drug price negotiation framework from the Inflation Reduction Act despite repeated court challenges. It also proposed rolling back hospital Conditions of Participation, a move estimated to save $320 million, including reversals of Biden-era emergency department obstetric care requirements. STAT notes that Democrats are debating how far to push on health care after their election win, and a former DOJ fraud chief expects closer scrutiny of industry ownership and payment structures from the new Congress. Hims & Hers has struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer its branded obesity drugs, and Fierce's new oral GLP-1 tracker shows Lilly's Foundayo setting a prescription record while Novo's Wegovy pill returns to its prior high. Omada raised its 2026 outlook after what it called its strongest quarter ever. Novo's longtime CFO is leaving at year-end, and an opinion piece argues CVS's planned split doesn't fix its core problem.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia dominated the open. Chief executive Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with an executive suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the board has opened an investigation into whether secrets were shared, per the WSJ. Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. Shares were down close to 5% premarket, and Bloomberg put the damage at about $200 billion of market value. The NYT reports that Secretary of State Rubio helped draft a secret memo this past spring warning officials about the relationship. Separately, the NYT says the Commerce Department cleared Nvidia H200 chips for dozens of Chinese companies, some with empty offices or ties to sanctioned firms. MarketWatch says Wall Street's first reaction was to wonder who would succeed Huang if he were forced out. Nvidia is too large and too central to the AI trade for this to stay a single-stock story, but the facts of the probe are still thin.

paragraphs.text: The backdrop was already fragile. The FT says global stocks were steady this morning after last week's AI rout, which pushed many indices into bear market territory. Asian equities mostly rebounded, although South Korean and Taiwanese authorities had stepped in to stem losses and sentiment is still fragile. Bloomberg says China's state-led funds bought a record amount of ETFs last week, and European indexes were little changed in quiet trading. Citi strategists cut US stocks and global tech and upgraded Europe on its lower AI exposure, saying tech positioning needs to get cleaner before they turn positive again. Morgan Stanley's chief strategist thinks the correction is in its final phase but advises waiting, since the S&P 500 could fall to the low end of its downside target in coming weeks. The FT says SoftBank's AI bet is under pressure ahead of its earnings.

paragraphs.text: In commodities and rates, oil fell below $100 after Trump played down new Iran strikes, though attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker incidents in Hormuz keep the risk alive. Bloomberg adds that crude slipped further on an unconfirmed report that Iran eased its Hormuz demands, so treat that move with caution. Gold rose above $4,100 an ounce as lower oil eased inflation worries, with US inflation data due this week. Barrick said higher gold and copper prices lifted third-quarter net earnings slightly. US and eurozone yields turned higher after earlier declines. ING thinks the euro's recent drop looks overdone given short-term rate differentials. China's factory-gate prices hit a four-year high for an eighth straight month, driven by oil and tech exports, while domestic demand stays weak. German exports rebounded in September but import growth narrowed the surplus.

paragraphs.text: Politics and central banks matter too. Euro-zone finance ministers began assessing the race to succeed Lagarde, with Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the two candidates. Knot told the FT he would act in a debt crisis, including by inventing new tools. The WSJ says Democratic election gains put Wall Street critics in key committee seats, but the Fed holds the real power over banks, and a Democratic Senate would be the broadest check yet on the president's efforts to control the central bank. Berkshire's third quarter was overshadowed, MarketWatch says, by poor Geico results, despite $357 billion of cash. Norway paused new data center power connections, a small sign of the grid strain behind AI spending.

paragraphs.text: Private credit supervision is the main theme. Alternative Credit Investor says the Australian regulator has halted two Angas private credit funds, and the Business Times reports the regulator stopped a private credit fund over risks tied to Bathla. Michael West Media says the Bathla lender blames a spreadsheet error for the stop order. The headlines don't say how these stories connect, so the cause and scale remain unclear. Still, regulators acting on retail-facing private credit vehicles are worth watching for contagion into redemptions and fundraising elsewhere.

Simply Wall Street says Morgan Stanley is exploring shifting data center loan risk to private credit, which fits the pattern of AI infrastructure financing being syndicated to non-bank buyers. A separate piece on Apollo's European credit launch shows managers still expanding. An opinion piece in RealClearMarkets warns of private credit's risks to savings and banking, and the Straits Times says big investors keep chasing private market deals, including in Singapore, despite risks and slower exits. Details are light on all of these.

paragraphs.text: Public credit looked steadier. Moomoo's Market Talk says euro credit spreads tightened even with heavy issuance, which suggests demand is absorbing supply despite the equity wobble. On the lending side, BBB and NatWest are backing UK lender Capital on Tap with £200 million. The NYT recounts how the collapse of Paraguay's Ueno bank ensnared President Santiago Peña, with prosecutors alleging nearly a billion dollars of government funds were funneled to the bank while executives made reckless insider loans. Those are accusations, and the piece is a case study in insider-lending risk. A Kalkine explainer on the Vanguard VCHY high-yield ETF is background only.

paragraphs.text: European bank consolidation is moving on several fronts. Crédit Agricole proposed merging its Italian business with Banco BPM. The FT says this would create Italy's third-largest bank, and the WSJ says Banco BPM would remain the listed entity in Milan. The FT also says UniCredit is set to seal its Commerzbank takeover this month and plans to restructure the German target in the first quarter of 2027. Intesa has Italian regulator approval for its $39.05 billion bid for Monte dei Paschi, with the offer due to launch later this month. Together these show cross-border and domestic bank M&A running at a high pace, which matters for advisory fees and financing.

The FT says BC Partners wants control of LIV Golf by buying the Saudi wealth fund's bankruptcy loan, a distressed-style route to the league's assets. MTN says its IHS Towers acquisition remains on track to close by year-end. WSJ's Heard on the Street says Boeing's deal losses are coming into sharper view, with no detail beyond that. The FT notes foreign buyers have taken over companies worth half a trillion pounds in UK takeovers over the past decade.

paragraphs.text: On the equity side, Windward Bio plans a Nasdaq IPO of up to $185 million, with an indicated price range of $16 to $18 per share. MakeMyTrip's India arm has Sebi approval to float an IPO, and Seeking Alpha says Wonder is bidding to list as part of a food delivery shake-up. Coinpedia says SpaceX stock, ticker SPCX, is trading near its IPO price with Jim Cramer flagging lock-up expiry risk; that is a thin source, so verify elsewhere. Robinhood has launched commission-free US IPO access for UK retail investors, and a Dangote official explained why its refinery IPO missed its 10 million investor target. The issuance window looks open for some biotechs and tech names but depends on this week's tone. Finally, the NYT tells the story of Weil Gotshal, a profitable firm that fell apart partly because it didn't adapt to Big Law's eat-or-be-eaten culture.
